utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Would the Registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-03-69-PT, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the record, could I have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. For the Prosecution, Alex Whiting, who is the new STA on this case; David Re, trial attorney; my name is Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff; and we are accompanied by Lakshime Walpita, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. For the Defence of Mr. Stanisic, Mr. Geert-Jan Knoops and my legal assistant Ms. Melinda Taylor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Zoran Jovanovic. I'm an attorney-at-law from Belgrade and I appear for the accused Franko Simatovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I think there are several motions outstanding, however, I don't think there is much to be done today in this Status Conference. First of all, I have to note that there is a motion to amend the indictment, and there's another motion for a joinder, the latter being considered by the Joinder Chamber, so I have nothing to say in relation to that motion. I note the Prosecution position to be that the motion to amend the indictment would not be affected by the motion for joinder. However, I note -- I was informed that Prosecution would seek to drop certain charges and reduce the crime base if the joinder was to be -- is to be granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. But we -- in any event, we would maintain the Srebrenica amendment. It would be related to other minor crime bases where there is no overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I heard. Speaking for myself, would it not be more efficient and convenient for the Chamber, as well as for the parties, to consider the motion to joinder after the -- I beg your pardon. How did I say? To consider the motion to amend the indictment after the motion for joinder is resolved? Do you have any observation on that matter?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: As the Srebrenica amendment is not affected by the joinder application, I wouldn't say that it's necessarily so, but whatever the Trial Chamber decides, we are going with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the joinder is to be granted, there would be an order to -- to the Prosecution to file a consolidated indictment, and then the current incumbent -- current indictment will be not operative any more, and then it will be more efficient to deal with the new indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me -- Your Honour, let me say in this context that we had a similar situation in the Seselj case, where we also had applied for an amendment despite the fact that we at the same time asked for joinder, and this was actually decided upon, and the Trial Chamber in the Seselj case granted the amendment, and we have next week an initial appearance of Mr. Seselj in relation to this amendment. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There are other items other than Srebrenica in the motion for the amendment of the indictment, so that cannot be -- it may be unnecessary to be dealt with in the interim.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I only wanted to point out that it was a similar situation and the Trial Chamber decided different from what your suggestion is. And we would actually appreciate to get a decision on the amendment, but if you would rather wait ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Of course I will -- the Chamber will consider the matter, but I don't think every Chamber has to follow the same course of action. Can I hear any observation from the Defence on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in our view, it would be efficient to act in this way. As for the two motions of the Prosecution, I believe we have already responded to both motions. At one point the Defence announced that it would seek leave to continue expressing its views on the motion for joinder should the Chamber so decide that the amendments be -- that the joinder be made. Although there are similarities, we feel that this would -- there would not be grounds for this. We feel that it would be correct after the decision on the joinder is made to issue a decision on an amendment to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic. Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in this stage we would like only to observe that the suggestion put forward should be also seen in the context of the interest of justice, because it's the question whether there is sufficient overlap in the crime bases regarding the respective defendants. And moreover, with respect to our case, a decision on the amendment could impact on the joinder, and vice versa, considering the pending medical issue we pointed to in our Rule 65 ter brief of last Tuesday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Knoops. Since you raised the issue of -- the medical issue, to be frank, I don't follow the point of yours raising the medical issue at the Status Conference. So are you going to file a motion to change the condition of provisional release, or what? Could you clarify it or elucidate on that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Your Honours seek to have further clarification on the exact ramifications of our observations last Tuesday, I would prefer to go into private session. If my information should go beyond the announcement of the filing of the medical motion with the relief sought which I elaborated on during the Rule 65 ter Conference last Tuesday, I have to go into more details, and then it would be probably more appropriate to do that in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't remember what I heard in relation to your ramification, but let's go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are there any matters to discuss in relation to disclosure? Any observation from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I can happily report back from the last Status Conference -- Your Honour will, of course, have read the transcript of the Rule 65 ter Conference on Tuesday -- the 66(A)(i) is still complete, as it was last time. 66(A)(ii) we have uncovered, with the assistance, and we're indebted to Mr. Jovanovic, an extra interview of a witness. We are disclosing that, as indeed another interview with another witness. So there were two things outstanding there which have come to our attention in the last few days. In relation to the next one, Rule 68 and the search terms, Defence counsel for Mr. Stanisic has provided us with search terms. We are utilising those in our searches of the remaining material not available to the Defence, namely the interviews -- sorry, the witness statements and the Rule 70 material which the OTP has exclusive access to at the moment. So we are in the process of doing that. The Rule 66(B), I don't think there are any issues arising from that. The next one was the Rule 94 bis, the exhumation reports. The translations are still being requested but we are at the moment reviewing whether or not they are required as they were used in Milosevic -- it's solved. I'm sorry. There is good news on that front. I have some very good news to report: Everything is translated and it's all on the EDS, and I apologise for the miscommunication by counsel at the bar table. The next one was access to transcripts and materials from the Milosevic case. Pursuant to the Trial Chamber's order of March this year, we have completed contacting all the witnesses in Milosevic who gave evidence in closed session relevant to the Stanisic and Simatovic aspects of the Milosevic indictments. Those who have consented to our providing the transcripts and exhibits to the Defence, we have done so now. We did that this week. We have reviewed the transcript of the remaining witnesses who did not consent to our providing the transcript to the Defence to see whether we could unredact or disclose parts in closed session. Unfortunately, there -- we were -- not unfortunately. The trial attorneys or the attorneys in Milosevic were so careful only to go into closed session on matters which would identify the witnesses that we are unable to disclose anything further because it would in fact identify those witnesses. The last matter which relates to disclosure was the list of suspect interviews provided by Defence counsel for Mr. Simatovic. That's Mr. Jovanovic. We have gone through the list and have now disclosed, mostly today and I think some earlier this week, all of the suspect interviews which we have found on that list. There are, I think, three or four we are still checking into on the basis that we are unsure whether there is a record of having spoken to those people as opposed to there being a transcribed suspect interview. So to up to the date, disclosure is as good as we can do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Re. That will be noted. I wonder if there are any observations on the part of the Defence on this issue of disclosure. Yes, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Just as my learned friend Mr. Re said, the Defence request under Rule 68 has been partly met. The only thing I would like to learn is: At the 65 ter Conference, the OTP said that it would have another military expert, Reynaud Theunens, from the Milosevic case. I would like to learn more details, if possible, about this. The Defence is familiar to a certain extent, in accordance with your decision on access to materials from the Milosevic case, that this is accompanied by a large number of documents. What I wish to know is whether these documents will be disclosed separately or whether the OTP will ask for an amendment to the list of exhibits. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was handed over the transcript of 65 ter Conference only this morning, so frankly, I didn't have enough time to go through all of it, but I'm of the understanding that the expert witnesses are five for the Prosecution. So you are going to add Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We actually plan to consolidate the witness and exhibits list in the near future, immediately, actually, after we know whether the cases are joined or not. Even if the cases are not joined and Stanisic and Simatovic would run alone, we think that for the Croatia part of this indictment, we would need a military expert detailing the military structures in Croatia, and that is actually Mr. Theunens who did that in the Milosevic case and who is already an expert witness in the Martic case and in the Seselj case. We would like to add this, and we -- we are able to disclose the materials immediately. That should not be a problem. But I wonder, as long as such an amendment to our witness list and exhibits list isn't granted, I wonder whether you already want to go through the materials. If you want to have them right now, it can be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it from the Defence submission it wishes to receive it as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. All documents accompanying the expert report of Reynaud Theunens is something that the Defence would like to have disclosed as soon as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic. Any observation, Mr. Knoops?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We -- despite the solution of several disclosure matters during the Rule 65 ter Conference last Tuesday, we respectfully ask your attention for two additional disclosure issues. One is more an information for Your Honours relating to Rule 66 disclosure. Today, in accordance with the outcome of the Rule 65 ter Conference of last Tuesday, the Defence in the Stanisic case did file its motion regarding the witness B24 in relation to the B/C/S transcripts. Secondly, that relates --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That would be considered by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes. Secondly, Your Honour, relating to Rule 66 and/or Rule 68 disclosure, we have an additional query regarding the Milosevic disclosure, and on this issue we are also willing to file a motion, if Your Honours would seek that we do so, but before we do so, we think it's proper to bring this today to the attention of Your Honours and the Prosecution. Of course we understand that formally the matter of the Milosevic disclosure is seized of by the Milosevic Chamber, but as the Chamber, as Your Honour knows himself, is composed of the same Judges as Judges in the Stanisic-Simatovic case and the Prosecution is also composed of the same trial attorneys, we think it's proper to bring this matter to your attention. As Your Honours may have noticed during the last Rule 65 ter Conference on Tuesday, the Prosecution indicated that in some cases where the witness in question would not consent to full disclosure of their statements to the Stanisic Defence, the Prosecution would not be able to disclose the private sessions of their testimony and, therefore, would also not be possible for the Prosecution to redact the statements further. In this situation, the Defence in the Stanisic case is put before a dilemma. On the one hand, we understand the position of the Prosecution; but on the other hand, Your Honours have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just pausing there. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, is it due to the order of delayed disclosure?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In these disclosure issues, I would like to have the questions addressed to Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it's actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Redaction is necessary?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's the terms of the Trial Chamber's order of the 11th of March, 2005, order 1(ii) says: "Where such consent is not given by the witness, the Prosecution has redacted those parts of the testimony and exhibits that may reveal the identity of any protected person or that relate to a period other than 1 April 1991 to 31 December 1995." The problem is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the identity of the witness will be disclosed to the Defence until certain deadline before the trial begins or before the actual witness comes to the Court to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There are two issues: The second part of the Pre-Trial Chamber's order relates to witnesses in Milosevic who are not on the witness list here in this particular case. We were to contact all of those in closed session. We did that. The majority said, yes, you can provide the testimony, and a small portion said we can't. Now, the Trial Chamber's order is go through it and, if you can deredact it, unredact it, provide it. I've gone through it, read it all; gone to the exhibits. Most of the exhibits relate to the identity of the witnesses. Unless the Trial Chamber changes its order, we're stuck with that. Of course, going through it, I found one Rule 68 matter, but -- in one of those witnesses, but we interpreted that as being subject to the protective 30 days before Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. trial order, but we could revisit that one later. So as it stands at the moment, the way the order is worded, our hands our tied. There is nothing to stop the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that order being an order of Pre-Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's -- the Pre-Trial Chamber of the Stanisic -- sorry, the Milosevic -- Milosevic, not Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's exactly the dilemma I refer to. At this moment, the Defence is not aware about the identities, first of all, of these witnesses and cannot assess the relevance of their statements and the portions which are apparently not disclosed yet. The rationale for the position of the Prosecution was that it had curtailed the use of private sessions for these witnesses to only those portions of the testimony for which it was strictly necessary. And it is our interpretation of the order of Your Honours that the identity may be not be revealed at this stage but it cannot extend to the entire contents of the particular statements. Unless Your Honours would interpret that order otherwise, we would suggest that, by way of compensation, the Prosecution were to verify with the Trial Chamber on an ex parte basis that it is not possible to redact the testimony in question further, and at the very least, we believe that the Prosecution should inform the Defence of the identity using pseudonyms or -- if that's necessary, of those witnesses which are relevant to the Stanisic case with which the Prosecution has not disclosed. Therefore, by this mechanism the Defence would be put in place to request further orders if needed. We cannot exclude that exculpatory evidence is part of those portions which -- to which the witness apparently didn't consent yet but which goes against the rationale of Your Honours' order, especially the order where Your Honours say, "Where such consent is not given by the witness, the Prosecution has redacted those parts of the testimony in exhibits that may reveal the identity." It doesn't say that it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Knoops, you would not challenge that the Chamber, as well as the Prosecution, have the obligation to protect the identity of the witnesses who was given a protective measure already and who are not to come to the Court as witnesses to its case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: We're not challenging that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But what you are saying is that with that redaction you cannot understand the case of the true content of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. It's our position that, without having access to the full statement, the Defence cannot understand the context of those portions which are disclosed, and the Defence, secondly, cannot exclude the possibility that exculpatory evidence is available in those portions which are not revealed by the Prosecution yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's a separate matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, but that makes for us part of the interpretation of the order of the Honourable Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So Stanisic Defence is going to file a motion in relation to this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: If that's the feeling of Your Honours, we will do, unless the Prosecution is willing to adopt our suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I was just speaking off the top of my head. Without an informed discussion, the Chamber is not able to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: In that regard, I think it's appropriate that we file a motion on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any comment from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it needs to be filed with the Milosevic Trial Chamber because that's the Trial Chamber who made the order. And when it comes to Rule 68 exculpatory materials, of course we disclose all the exculpatory material we come across. And if we can't give the actual wording of a certain protected testimony, we at least give the information in a memo form. So I can't really understand why you would -- why you think you need to have the exact parts that are protected when we know there is no exculpatory material in it and when we provide the exculpatory parts, as Mr. Re said to you, in the proper form that we are allowed to do. I can't really see where the dispute comes from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: However, if that very witness is going to testify in the Stanisic case, the Prosecution will disclose the identity and the redacted part at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. For the witnesses that are actually witnesses in this case here, there is no problem at all because this information will be disclosed 30 days before the trial starts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will consider the Defence assertion if filed later. Is there any matter to raise for the parties?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Not from the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: From the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] None from the Defence, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. None from the Defence in the Stanisic case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One matter is in relation to agreed facts. I've read the filings from the parties, and after I have seen the Defence response that -- in which they said that they cannot agree to any of the proposed facts except for the date of birth, and I asked the Prosecution to file their questions. I haven't gone through in detail, but my first impression is that the Prosecution was too ambitious to get the agreed facts as much as possible. And the counter-proposal was the same, and I wonder whether we can start from these minor facts. For example, I'm very pleased to hear that the translation issue in relation to exhumation report has been resolved, but I wonder whether we can start from those things, some certain bodies were exhumed from certain place, setting aside the cause of death and -- but because we are going to deal with the joinder issue and at this moment it would be more efficient as well to put on hold the further negotiation in agreed facts, while I would very much encourage the parties negotiation further, but let us leave the matter as it is right now. So -- and then the next Status Conference will be held either at the end of December or in the middle of January, which will be announced in due course. And having said that, the hearing is now adjourned.
